    40% off: activations +31%, rev +18%, SMB tier, sample 12 billing periods; pricing page otherwise unaltered.

    Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.

CURRENT SITUATION — day 76

  Three things are happening at once:

  Primary objective: maximize sustainable long-term qualified revenue.

  Analyst time is limited. You may pull the archived source record for at most

memory_block.body: 40% off: activations +31%, rev +18%, SMB tier, sample 12 billing periods; pricing page otherwise unaltered.
Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.
Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.
Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.
Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.
Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.

answer.rationale:
The two symptoms actually degrading (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point directly at the funnel, not at price. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the tempting response to the competitor, but that memory is the one I trust least on its face: a 40% discount reporting +18% revenue over only 12 billing periods measures the window in which discounted cohorts have not yet had to renew at full price, and it says nothing about retention, expansion, or cohort quality. Discount-led acquisition against a cheaper entrant also risks re-anchoring SMB price expectations permanently, which cuts against 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue.' So I am not spending scarce verification on the option I do not intend to run.

I am spending both pulls on memory_31 and memory_86 because they are the load-bearing support for the action I do intend, and because they may not be two pieces of evidence at all. 'Signup simplification improved SMB activation' (day 12) and 'shortening onboarding improved completion and time-to-value' (day 52) could plausibly be two consolidations of the same underlying experiment, or nested slices of one program. If so, my apparent double confirmation collapses to a single result and I should scale down. The archive pull is the only way to distinguish independent replication from duplicated summary. I also want the original records' scope: memory_31 is explicitly SMB, memory_86 says 'self-serve accounts,' and I need to know whether the measured lift was activation-rate only or carried through to qualified revenue.

Standing caveat regardless of what the archive returns: cutting required signup fields is exactly the kind of change that lifts the top-of-funnel metric while degrading what arrives downstream — fewer qualification fields can mean lower lead quality and worse routing, and memory_44 says enterprise pipeline quality depends on the sales-assisted path. So the experiment must be guarded: segment to self-serve SMB only so it cannot cannibalize the enterprise demo-request route, hold out a control, and instrument to qualified-revenue and 30/90-day retention rather than stopping at completion rate. If either verified record turns out to be short-horizon or a duplicate of the other, I drop to a small guarded test rather than proceeding at this scale. Activation messaging (memory_91) is the fallback if onboarding evidence does not survive verification; referral incentives (memory_57) address established customers and do not touch the failing stage.
